title: Margaret Hagan & Sateesh Nori — putting AI to the test for legal services: lab-to-pilot pipelines and the crisis case for urgency
pub: Talk Justice, An LSC Podcast, episode 82, host Cat Moon (Vanderbilt), YouTube / Legal Talk Network
author: Margaret Hagan · Sateesh Nori

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI could expand legal help while emphasizing that experimentation is not yet proof of sustained access-to-justice gains. It materially develops the proposition by proposing a community-informed research-to-demonstration pipeline, shared infrastructure, empirical evaluation and legal-domain safeguards for moving from promising use cases to accountable deployment.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core case for selective, human-centred and evidence-led deployment, then materially extends it with concrete access-to-justice workflows—especially intake, triage, paperwork, litigant coaching and pro bono copilots—and a proposal to evaluate pilots against imperfect existing services. Its urgency is tempered by explicit recognition that deployment remains experimental and requires empirical validation, coordination and legal-domain guardrails.

And we need empirical data as well as voices from people like Satish and other folks who are doing innovative work responsibly, cautiously, but still embracing the potential of generative AI to close the justice gap.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source supports using generative AI to expand access to civil legal help while pairing urgency with safe, intentional experimentation and collaboration. Its research updates and expectations do not provide measured access or outcome gains, reinforcing the cluster’s distinction between active experimentation and proven impact.

kp.k: Justice-gap urgency motivates deployment against realistic alternatives
kp.d: Nori argues that unmet civil legal need warrants immediate action rather than prolonged speculation about risks. He states that 92% of people's civil legal problems go unaddressed and estimates that New York City services fail to serve probably 50% or more of those needing them; the transcript supplies no underlying study for these figures. Reporting Dean Perlman's argument, Nori says innovations should be compared with existing, imperfect provision rather than an ideal service. He also argues that lawyers' risk aversion can obstruct implementation.
qs: 92% of people's civil legal problems are going unaddressed.
we are not serving probably 50% or more of the people who need our services.
We have a tool that works today. We've got to use it.
It seems to be that it's the perfect outcome that we're measuring this against, the perfect scenario, the perfect paralegal, the perfect model. That's not happening right now.

kp.k: User research precedes demonstration projects and shared infrastructure
kp.d: Hagan describes Stanford Legal Design Lab's first phase as interviews, scenario exercises in which people tried and rated AI, provider discussions, and a survey of frontline legal-help providers. This work explores appetite for legal problem-solving tools, priority tasks, quality and risks rather than establishing demonstrated service improvements. In spring 2024 she describes a transition toward demonstration R&D and nationwide networks supporting local projects. No sample sizes or quantitative survey results are given.
qs: that's meant doing a lot of interviews, scenario exercises where we have people try out AI and rate it, talking to providers about what kinds of tasks and opportunities they think should be prioritized
basically trying to identify an agenda of where AI might be useful or not and how to evaluate quality and risks for these prospective use cases.
we're excited to start doing some demonstration R&D projects and starting to build networks across the country

kp.k: Tenant-law prototypes offer anecdotal evidence, not validated performance
kp.d: Nori reports building about a dozen GPTs, including tools for analysing a rent-overcharge decision, drafting housing-condition complaint letters, guiding photographic documentation, and identifying possible mold. He judged seven of approximately eight analytical bullet points comparable to what an expert lawyer might produce and says a letter-writing GPT took about three minutes to build. These are personal experimental assessments, not systematic evaluations; he explicitly describes the mold result as less verifiable.
qs: including building about a dozen GPTs on ChatGPT to test out the use cases for Gen AI.
it gave me about eight bullet points, seven of which a really expert lawyer probably would come up with.
I built a GPT to help a tenant generate a letter to complain to their landlord about housing conditions. And that took about three minutes.
That was less kind of verifiable. But the model said, this could be mold.

kp.k: Housing hotline copilot augments relatively inexperienced operators
kp.d: Nori describes connecting the legal-tech company named Joseph in the transcript with Housing Court Answers, which receives about 50,000 tenant calls annually. A copilot supplies background answers to operators typically two to three years out of school, who relay them to callers. He presents a standalone chatbot as a possible later step, not current deployment, and conditions his prediction of transformative triage improvements on the copilot working.
qs: they get about 50,000 phone calls per year from tenants who are trying to get answers about their fights with their landlords.
they have operators who are typically two to three years out of school

we built a co-pilot model for these operators so that the Gen AI can be in the background, like a really experienced supervisor, and can feed answers to the person who can then relay them to the caller as a first step.
Eventually, maybe the Gen AI can stand on its own.
But for now, we're using it as a co-pilot.

kp.k: Information delivery, pro bono support and intake are priorities
kp.d: Nori identifies three near-term opportunities: providing legal information and advice through the digital channels people use, helping pro bono lawyers navigate unfamiliar legal areas, and reducing labor-intensive intake. His hypothetical tax lawyer taking an immigration case illustrates potential capacity expansion through assistance, not established competence gains. He describes repeated data entry, queues and staff burnout as intake problems. Host Moon separately reports that Legal Aid of North Carolina's Innovation Lab reframes intake as access and triage, including for people the organization cannot represent.
qs: What I'm excited about is three areas. One is legal information and advice.
Now you can build a pro bono co-pilot to help a lawyer understand immigration issues and navigate them forward and expand access to justice in that way.

Right now, it requires hours and hours of effort, people waiting in lines, filling out paper forms, those forms being entered into a database, that database being re-entered into a funder database, and so on.
they are actually reframing intake as access.

kp.k: Provider surveys prioritize case entry and paperwork
kp.d: Hagan reports that surveyed legal-aid workers, court-help staff and law librarians identify early-case assistance and paperwork as especially impactful and feasible uses. Early-case support includes answering questions, issue spotting, plain-language or preferred-language guidance, explaining the legal journey and matching service providers. Paperwork opportunities include translating users' accounts and evidence into forms or letters and accelerating the back-end creation of accessible digital tools. These are reported preferences and proposed capabilities, not measured outcomes.
qs: the most excitement that we've seen from them, what they see as one of the biggest impactful and feasible priorities for Gen AI, is all about, I would say, two hot zones.
Getting basic questions answered, issues spotting, getting that in the right plain English language or language of choice
The other hot zone that is really a priority of the community from the survey is all around paperwork.

Can that process of creating form and letter writing tools really be supercharged so that we have a new generation of very accessible modern form filling tools or letter making tools like Satish was already saying?

kp.k: AI coaching could connect fragmented unbundled legal services
kp.d: Hagan anticipates that many litigants will continue combining clinics, court self-help centers, lawyer-for-a-day programs and their own work rather than receiving full representation. She proposes AI as a continuing coach or copilot that could maintain orientation and engagement across these fragmented journeys. This is an opportunity she is personally excited about, not a finding from the provider survey or a demonstrated intervention.
qs: people have to kind of cobble together some services at a clinic with something at a self-help center at a court, with something at a lawyer for a day program.
that can be very disorienting and confusing and hard to stay engaged with.
if generative AI can help be kind of a copilot and a coach for that person, that litigant, especially going through a longer legal journey to keep them on track

kp.k: Task-specific laboratory evaluation should precede supervised field pilots
kp.d: Hagan proposes university-based technical development and expert assessment of specific tasks, comparing AI-generated answers, letters or forms with the best available human work on quality and time. Matching or exceeding that standard would trigger controlled copilot trials with humans strongly involved in spotting, recording and correcting problems. Unlike Nori's broad critique of perfection-based comparisons, her proposed operational threshold explicitly refers to best available human performance. She stresses that field trials reveal performance and risk issues unavailable from laboratory testing alone.
qs: Can the AI system beat or match the quality of the best available human?
When we have experts come and rate the AI's response or letter or form compared to kind of the human created, can AI match or beat it on the quality and on the efficiency, the time to take to do it?
then it's time to go to the co-pilot phase, where we're rolling it out with a human, strongly in the loop, using this AI, but having a lot of ability to spot problems, record those, correct the AI
we're not gonna know performance issues or risk issues until we start doing controlled pilots in the field.

kp.k: Measured risks should guide public release and iterative protections
kp.d: Hagan recommends measuring hallucinations and bias in controlled pilots before considering controlled direct-to-public release. She argues that consumer protections and deployment rules should develop iteratively from observed performance and risks rather than predictions made in spring 2024. No hallucination or bias rates are reported. Her approach seeks to preserve experimentation while responding to demonstrated harms.
qs: How often does it hallucinate? How often does bias get exhibited?
Let's actually measure that instead of speculating.
then to think about controlled release straight to the public, like kind of in the hands of the consumer or the public.
rather than trying to sit right now as of spring 2024 and foresee the risks and problems and make regulations based on that
responsible R&D that is pushing forward, is not chilling the space, but is still making sure there are consumer protections for the risks that do emerge.

kp.k: Empirical evidence should inform platform policies and legal regulation
kp.d: Hagan argues that open consumer access to AI already permits legal queries with few domain-specific guardrails. She recommends coordinating research and practitioner voices to influence both model/platform companies and state bars or court task forces. She warns that prominent failures and speculative risk narratives could influence restrictive policies, including platforms ceasing to answer legal questions. Whether access will remain open a year later is explicitly uncertain; value should be demonstrated only if it exists.

We need to make sure that there are research studies that do show or prove the value if it exists
those folks are the ones who can put the guard rails up, allowing the kind of power of AI with some guard rails specific for the legal domain.
whether that's state bars in the different states or the kind of court task forces that are forming
We don't know what that future will hold

kp.k: National collaboration can strengthen locally tailored pilots
kp.d: Hagan recommends formal or informal national cohorts sharing vendor-selection experience, data structuring, quality assurance, system design, emerging risks and sustainability practices. She expects substantial local AI work to remain necessary within the US system but argues that shared knowledge can improve its speed and quality. Nori supplies an urgency analogy to pandemic vaccine collaboration among academia, government and private organizations; it is an argument for coordination, not evidence that legal AI will achieve comparable outcomes.
qs: Once we can kind of share a lot of this strategic knowledge about vendor relationships, data structuring, quality assurances, all these things that you need to think about if you're gonna launch a pilot, we can start supercharging local pilots across the country
We're gonna have to do a lot of local AI work
these kind of informal or formal national cohorts that we're learning and also chatting with each other regularly about the risks we're seeing
academia and the government and the private sector in the form of pharmaceutical companies and hospitals got together and they put out vaccines
We need to act with an urgency that I don't think we're used to in the legal space.

kp.k: Treat generative AI as inspiration rather than an oracle
kp.d: Nori's practical recommendation is to experiment with AI as a source of ideas for changing practice and service delivery, rather than treating it as an authoritative predictor or automatic replacement for lawyers' existing work. He includes document assembly, pro bono, collaboration, document review and legal research among the activities it might inspire practitioners to rethink. He explicitly allows that experimentation may yield useful ideas without eventual AI adoption.
qs: I think the trap is to see it as an oracle
Instead, I would encourage folks to say, Gen AI is a muse.
Look at the ways that it can inspire us to change the way we practice law, the way we deliver legal services
Or maybe I don't use it, but it will give me some ideas and will help me keep going

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nori presents generative AI as an immediately usable way to expand civil legal assistance; Hagan identifies promising uses and advocates a staged, empirically tested route to deployment.
pts.d: Nori reports that his experimental GPTs identified weaknesses in a complex New York rent-overcharge decision, generated tenant complaint letters, and guided tenants in photographing housing conditions. He describes a Housing Court Answers copilot built with the legal-tech company called Joseph in the transcript: it supplies answers to hotline operators, who relay them to callers. He predicts that, if successful, this could transform resource-intensive legal-services triage; a standalone public chatbot is a possible later step, not the current deployment. He identifies three immediately implementable opportunities: conversational delivery of legal information and advice, copilots enabling lawyers to undertake pro bono matters outside their usual specialty, and intake assistance reducing repetitive forms, database entry, queues, and staff workload. Hagan similarly anticipates increased capacity within constrained legal-aid resources. She identifies early-case guidance, issue spotting, plain-language or preferred-language explanations, matching people to providers, and paperwork as priority applications. She suggests AI could both simplify users' production of forms and letters and reduce the backend work needed to create accessible digital tools. Separately, she proposes AI coaching to keep self-represented litigants oriented and engaged as they piece together unbundled services. Hagan also predicts that sharing technical designs, vendor knowledge, data practices, and quality-assurance methods through national cohorts could accelerate local pilots and improve their quality. Her lab-to-pilot pathway is a proposed method for establishing capability and risks, not a finding that AI already meets its proposed performance standard. Nori's closing framing is augmentation and inspiration rather than reliance on AI as an authoritative oracle or a general replacement for lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The offered basis is practitioner experimentation, frontline-provider research, and descriptions of an early copilot project; the episode reports no completed comparative evaluation or measured access-to-justice improvement.
pts.d: Nori draws on approximately 22 years representing low-income New Yorkers and personal experimentation with about a dozen custom GPTs. For the rent-overcharge decision, he judges seven of eight generated criticisms comparable to what an expert lawyer might identify; this is his assessment of one example, not a benchmark result. He says building a tenant complaint-letter GPT took about three minutes and that it works well, without reporting a systematic evaluation. His photograph-based mold experiment is expressly less verifiable; he welcomes the model's qualified suggestion to investigate further. For Housing Court Answers, he reports about 50,000 annual calls and operators typically two to three years out of school. These figures describe the service context, not demonstrated AI productivity or accuracy gains. Hagan reports interviews, scenario exercises in which participants tried and rated AI, and a survey of legal-aid, court-help, and library personnel. She says respondents prioritized early-case assistance and paperwork as impactful and feasible applications, but supplies no sample sizes, numerical results, or measured task outcomes. Her proposed expert-rated comparisons of AI and human work, efficiency measurements, and field measurements of hallucinations and bias are future evaluation plans. Nori also invokes the justice crisis, asserting that 92% of people's civil legal problems go unaddressed and that New York City probably fails to serve at least half of those needing its services. The episode does not identify the underlying study or population definition for the 92% statement. These figures support his urgency argument, not proof of AI effectiveness. Predictions about pro bono expansion, reduced intake burdens, coaching, and national collaboration are reasoned proposals rather than reported outcome findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion is situated in spring 2024: Nori stresses immediate experimentation, while Hagan conditions wider deployment on task-specific testing and progressively supervised pilots.
pts.d: At the time of the episode, Nori describes personal prototypes and the Housing Court Answers copilot as already built, while triage transformation remains conditional on the copilot working successfully. He regards information delivery, pro bono support, and intake applications as available for implementation now. His urgency argument calls for judging innovation against existing unmet need and imperfect services rather than an idealized perfect service. Hagan says the Legal Design Lab is moving from background research begun the previous spring into demonstration R&D and national networking. Her proposed sequence is: develop a strong task-specific system in a lab; compare quality and completion time against the best available human performance; proceed to a controlled field copilot when the lab comparison is positive; maintain a human strongly in the loop to identify, record, and correct problems; and consider controlled direct-to-public release after observing performance and risks. She does not predict a date for widespread deployment. She argues that field pilots are needed to reveal otherwise unanticipated risks and that protections should evolve with observed evidence rather than speculative risk forecasts. She also warns that the relatively open availability of legal answers from general-purpose AI could change through platform policies or regulation. Her one-year horizon is explicitly uncertain: she does not know whether platforms will remain open or be pushed to stop answering legal questions. Empirical research and coordinated practitioner input are proposed conditions for informing those decisions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The anticipated benefits concern unmet civil legal need and public-interest service capacity, rather than commercial law-firm economics or lawyer displacement.
pts.d: For low-income tenants, Nori anticipates more accessible housing-rights answers, complaint letters, evidence-gathering guidance, and triage. He also identifies people facing immigration problems, eviction, or wage violations as needing actionable answers urgently. For legal-aid clients and self-represented litigants generally, Hagan anticipates easier navigation, language-accessible guidance, less burdensome paperwork, better provider connections, and continuity across fragmented assistance. For hotline operators, legal-aid staff, court-help personnel, and law librarians, AI is principally an assistant intended to add capacity; operators remain intermediaries in the described Housing Court Answers project. For pro bono lawyers, Nori proposes specialty-specific support that could reduce apprehension about taking unfamiliar matters and expand available help. For nonprofit organizations, intake and triage applications are expected to reduce administrative burdens associated with scarce resources and burnout. For legal-aid technology groups, Hagan anticipates easier production of digital form and letter tools, with shared national learning supporting locally specific implementation. For the public using general-purpose models directly, Hagan identifies both an opportunity for accessible legal information and the risk of self-harm through inadequate safeguards. Technology companies, state bars, and court task forces are the decision-makers she wants informed by empirical evidence, because their policies could enable or constrain public access. Neither speaker supplies a prediction of legal-sector job losses, changes in firm staffing structures, or commercial pricing.
